newsitem.title: USA: Clintons, Gores begin inaugural in prayer.
newsitem.headline: Clintons, Gores begin inaugural in prayer.

text.p: At a church that once served as a safe house for runaway slaves, President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore listened to serenades, sermons and prayerful good wishes Monday at an inter-faith inaugural prayer service.
The singing, clapping and preaching went on for so long that Clinton, Gore and their families were late getting back to the White House for a pre-inaugural coffee with leaders of Congress.
The overflowing crowd of about 1,500 people at the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church heard religious readings from a rabbi, a Moslem imam and a Greek Orthodox archbishop.

But the most powerful performance was from the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who was with the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. when the civil rights leader was slain in Memphis in 1968. Monday marked the national holiday of King's birth.
Jackson urged Clinton not to ignore the plight of the poor and downtrodden, saying that King would say that, "It's not enough to lock them up, we must lift them up."

And for the oft-criticised first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, Jackson urged her to go on with her goal of expanding health care for more Americans. Her first-term effort to do so ended in a dismal failure.
"Miss Hillary don't let lesser men frighten people. Just keep up the dream of fighting for health care," he said. "You would dare be a giant! Don't let these Lilliputians ... pull you down."
He told Clinton and Gore not to forget the people who elected them.
"You were elected by the poor and the humble people," he said. "They elected you. You won Appalachia. You won Harlem. You won the barrios. You won the farm workers."
Interspersed between the prayers and preaching were rousing renditions of hymns. Mickey Mangun and the Messiah Singers had the crowd on its feet cheering with "Lift Up Holy Hands."
One of Clinton's long-time friends from Arkansas even performed. Carolyn Staley sang a solo of "Be Not Afraid," and at the end told the Clintons, "I love you. I love you."

The Rev. Bill Hybels of the Willow Creek Community Church of South Barrington, Ill., told the congregation that he has visited with Clinton once a month for nearly the entire four years of his first term to pray and discuss religious issues.
The Rev. Anthony Compolo urged Democrats and Republicans to set aside political acrimony and work together.

"This president is tired of the politics of bile. This speaker of the House (Newt Gingrich) is tired of the politics of bile. Enough of this accusing, and let's move on together, forgiving each other, even as God has forgiven us," Compolo said.

The Metropolitan A.M.E. Church once served as a stop on the Underground Railroad for slaves fleeing the South before and during the Civil War. Noted ex-slave and civil rights leader Frederick Douglass often spoke at the church and his funeral was there in 1895.
